1 Introduction

The accelerated growth of wearable devices has revolutionized the development of intelligent and integrated textile-based energy devices [1–5]. Self-powered textiles with integrated energy storage and sensors have been the focus of research attention for their prospective use in individual medical care, smart homes, and human-machine interaction [5–8]. For energy storage module, in contrast to the drawbacks of low power density and poor cycle life of batteries, the significant advantages of supercapacitors lie in superior power density, faster charging and discharging, and extended lifetime [9]. Generally, a self-powered textiles are supposed to enable precise measurement of signals without disturbances from body movements, which demands supercapacitor with strain-insensitivity to fit the curvature and activities of human body [10]. Currently, the supercapacitors for the self-powered textiles devices are primarily constructed from large-scale fabric structures, including MWCNT/MoO3 two-dimensional (2D) knitted textile [11] and MXene/Zn three-dimensional (3D) woven spacer fabric [12]. Although Su et al. [13] developed a one-dimensional (1D) braided thread using carbon nanotubes, polyester and rubber, the work suffers from difficulty in accurate sensing under stretching. Therefore, new materials and structure designs that have both electrochemical and sensing properties are desirable to increase the supercapacitors’ strain-insensitivity and sensors’ sensitivity of self-powered textiles for practical wearable applications.
